name: DIU (diu.mil): The Defense Innovation Unit's Commercial AI Project Catalog
title: DIU (diu.mil): The Defense Innovation Unit's Commercial AI Project Catalog
answer: The Defense Innovation Unit's website is the public record of how commercial AI enters U.S. military programs. Its project catalog describes contracted autonomy work in detail, including Overland AI's OverDrive and OverWatch systems for uncrewed ground vehicles, Applied Intuition's simulation toolchain for testing Army autonomy stacks, and C3.ai's fuel-optimization analytics for mobility airlift. It also publishes open solicitations, such as the Low Cost ISR challenge with a $100 million prize pool, giving vendors and observers a concrete view of what the department is buying.

sections.body: The Defense Innovation Unit publishes diu.mil, the public face of the only Department of War organization focused exclusively on fielding and scaling commercial technology across the U.S. military. The site combines a solutions overview, a portfolio catalog of contracted projects, and submission pages for open solicitations. The catalog entries read as project descriptions rather than marketing, each naming the commercial vendor, the military problem, and the technical approach. The pages reviewed were read on 2026-10-03 and cover projects spanning ground autonomy, simulation and test, mine countermeasures, aviation fuel analytics, and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The catalog's ground vehicle entries share a common problem statement: current U.S. military and uncrewed ground vehicle systems lack an integrated software architecture supporting both robust teleoperation and fully autonomous waypoint navigation in complex, contested environments. DIU contracted several vendors against that gap. Overland AI's OverDrive is a modular, vehicle-agnostic autonomy stack for off-road, communications-limited environments, paired with OverWatch, a tactical command and control interface letting one operator task and coordinate multiple vehicles. Forterra offers an integrated stack combining AutoDrive and a Vehicle-Level Planner, with an ATAK-compatible interface for dismounted and mounted use. Kodiak Robotics' Kodiak Driver combines multi-sensor perception, redundant control, and scalable AI, with embedded probabilistic risk assessment for continuous safety quantification. Applied Intuition's Autonomous Development Platform addresses the Army's need to test autonomy stacks in simulation, validating performance across parameterized scenarios and operational design domains. Greensea's Bayonet 250 was modified into an autonomous underwater ground vehicle for mine countermeasures in surf zones and on beaches, adding payload and towing capacity, a towed array sensor, autonomous navigation, automatic target recognition sensing, and edge compute. C3.ai's platform ingests historical and near-real-time mobility aircraft data to optimize flight paths and fuel use. The site also describes DIU's contracting mechanics and an open Low Cost ISR challenge.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: DIU states it leverages Other Transaction authority under 10 USC 4022 to award prototype agreements in as few as 60 to 90 days. Vendors completing a prototyping project satisfactorily receive a Success Memo, which lets them do business with any federal agency, including the Department of War, without competitive bid, with no time restriction on its use. The Predictive Maintenance solicitation opened in July 2017 for the U.S. Air Force, and by November 2019 the C3.ai prototype had transitioned to a production Other Transaction agreement. The site states the U.S. military consumes over 2 billion gallons of aviation fuel annually. The Low Cost ISR challenge awards a total prize and initial follow-on pool of $100 million, with up to $250 million budgeted for further development, production, and theater integration. Endurance bands are defined as medium, 3 to 12 or more hours, and long, 12 to 24 or more hours.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For anyone tracking AI in defense, this site is a working record of what the department actually buys from commercial vendors and under what terms. The catalog entries name the vendors, the operational problems, and the technical requirements, from autonomy stacks and simulation toolchains to automatic target recognition and fuel analytics. The contracting mechanics matter as much as the technology: the 60 to 90 day prototype timeline and the Success Memo pathway explain how a commercial AI company can move from a prototype to government-wide business without a competitive bid. The open Low Cost ISR solicitation shows the current demand signal, including autonomy features to reduce operator workload, modular open systems alignment with Project AVO, and navigation in GNSS-denied environments.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Defense

sections.body: The catalog pages are project descriptions written from the government's perspective, so they present vendor capabilities as stated in the contracting context rather than independent evaluations, and they give no performance results, deployment numbers, or cost figures for the individual projects. Several entries are dated by their project history, such as the Predictive Maintenance timeline ending in 2019. The site covers only DIU's own portfolio, not the broader defense AI market, and the solicitation pages describe desired characteristics that are not pass or fail requirements at initial submission.
